Empirical Research Plan – “Does Having More Children Reduce Parents’ Labor Supply?”

----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
----------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Two–Stage Least Squares (Instrumental‐Variables, IV)

Justification
• Endogenous regressor: total number of children (fertility) is jointly determined with parents’ labour‐supply preferences ⇒ OLS biased downward in absolute value.  
• Instrument: sex composition of the first two births (“same sex”) is as‐good‐as‐random, strongly predicts the probability of having a third birth (first stage ≈ 6 p.p.), and, conditional on controls, is uncorrelated with parents’ latent labour‐supply preferences.  
• A second, conceptually distinct, instrument – twins at parity-2 – provides an over-identification check.  
Because treatment intensity (number of children) varies and there is no clear running variable or policy discontinuity, IV is the appropriate causal design.

----------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
----------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
T = Total number of own children in the household (endogenous, integer).

Instrument(s)  
Z1 = SameSex12 ≡ 1 if first two children are both boys or both girls.  
Z2 = Twin2 ≡ 1 if second birth is a multiple (optional robustness & over-ID).

Control (counterfactual) group  
Parents whose first two children are mixed sex (boy–girl or girl–boy) form the primary control group for the SameSex12 instrument.

Timing  
We observe mothers aged 21–35 at the census date. By construction, all have at least two children already. The instrument affects whether they have progressed to a third birth by the census year.

----------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
----------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance – SameSex12 must raise the probability of having ≥3 children.  
Plausibility: Documented U.S. estimates show ~0.06–0.07 increase. Large sample gives F-stat > 10.

A2. Independence – Conditional on controls, SameSex12 is independent of the unobserved determinants of parents’ labour supply.  
Plausibility: Child sex is biologically random; U.S. 1980/1990 cohorts have negligible sex‐selective fertility or abortion.

A3. Exclusion Restriction – SameSex12 affects labour supply only through its effect on fertility, not through other channels (e.g., child-specific costs).  
Plausibility: Hard to violate; differential costs by sex composition (e.g., re-using clothes or bedrooms) are tiny relative to labour decisions.

A4. Monotonicity – Having two same-sex children weakly increases the likelihood of any parent having another child (no “defiers”).  
Plausibility: Virtually all preference models predict weakly monotone behaviour.

A5. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA) – One household’s sex composition does not affect another’s labour supply.  
Plausibility: Reasonable.

----------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
----------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential child-gender effects on labour supply unrelated to fertility (e.g., boys are “harder” or more expensive).  
Mitigation:  i)  Show that labour outcomes for parents of two children do not differ by sex composition when total fertility is fixed at 2 (placebo).  
              ii) Include controls for the sex of the first two children when focusing on twin instrument.

T2. Sample selection – Sample is married women aged 21–35; differential divorce or marriage market effects may correlate with sex composition.  
Mitigation:  i)  Replicate using the full set of women (married + unmarried) when possible.  
              ii) Control for marital status or restrict to couples intact since first two births (use “own‐children” linkage).

T3. Weak instrument for sub-groups – First-stage strength could vary by mother’s education or race.  
Mitigation:  i)  Report first-stage F-stats for each subgroup.  
              ii) Use LIML or Anderson–Rubin tests as robustness.

----------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
----------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)    # fast data handling
library(fixest)        # IV estimation
library(estimatr)      # robust SEs
library(modelsummary)  # neat tables

# 1. Load Data -----------------------------------------------
# Assume two csv files: pums80.csv and pums90.csv
pums80 <- fread("pums80.csv")
pums90 <- fread("pums90.csv")
pums   <- rbindlist(list(pums80, pums90), use.names = TRUE, fill = TRUE)

# 2. Sample restriction --------------------------------------
pums <- pums[
  female == 1 &                 # women
  age %between% c(21, 35) &     # age 21-35
  num_children >= 2 &           # at least two kids present
  married == 1                  # currently married
]

# 3. Variable construction -----------------------------------
# Sex of first two children: assuming variables child1_sex, child2_sex
pums[, same_sex12 := as.integer(child1_sex == child2_sex)]

# Twins at second birth
pums[, twin2 := as.integer(child2_multiple == 1)]

# Endogenous regressor
pums[, kids := num_children]     # total children

# Outcomes
pums[, lfp  := as.integer(weeks_worked > 0)]
pums[, hours := weeks_worked * hours_per_week]
pums[, ln_inc:= log(labor_income + 1)]

# Controls
pums[, c("age", "age_first_birth", "educ_yrs", "race_black", "race_hisp")]

# 4. Main IV regression --------------------------------------
# Example: effect on annual weeks worked
iv_formula <- weeks_worked ~ age + I(age^2) + age_first_birth + educ_yrs +
                             race_black + race_hisp |
                             . - kids + same_sex12

est_main <- feols(iv_formula, data = pums, cluster = ~statefip)
etable(est_main, se.below = TRUE)

# 5. First-stage check ---------------------------------------
fs <- feols(kids ~ same_sex12 + age + I(age^2) + age_first_birth + educ_yrs +
                        race_black + race_hisp, data = pums, cluster = ~statefip)
summary(fs)$iv_first_stage # F-statistics

# 6. Robustness: use twin instrument, over-ID J-test ----------
iv_2inst <- feols(weeks_worked ~ age + I(age^2) + age_first_birth + educ_yrs +
                                race_black + race_hisp |
                                . - kids + same_sex12 + twin2,
                  data = pums, cluster = ~statefip)
etable(list("Main" = est_main, "SS+Twin" = iv_2inst), se.below = TRUE)

# Placebo: restrict to women with exactly 2 children -----------
placebo <- feols(weeks_worked ~ same_sex12 + age + I(age^2) + age_first_birth +
                              educ_yrs + race_black + race_hisp,
                 data = pums[kids == 2], cluster = ~statefip)
summary(placebo)
```

----------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
----------------------------------------------------------------
Theory suggests additional children reduce mothers’ labour supply because of time-allocation and childcare costs; fathers’ labour supply may rise or stay constant (added-worker vs. household specialisation). Prior magnitudes from the literature: an extra child for U.S. mothers in the 1980s lowers annual weeks worked by ≈ 4–6 weeks (≈ 8–12 %) and hourly labour income by ≈ 5–10 %.

----------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
----------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Relevance (strong first stage) ………… 1  
C2: Independence (random assignment) …… 1  
C3: Exclusion restriction ………………… 0.5  (plausible but not testable)  
C4: Monotonicity ………………………… 1  
C5: SUTVA / no spillovers ………………… 1  

Total ≈ 4.5 / 5 – overall credible design, with the exclusion restriction the main unverifiable caveat.
